The university's main lecture hall was bigger than Giulia had imagined: three hundred seats, a dark wooden stage, a microphone and a huge screen behind the lectern. At ten to four almost all the seats were taken. There were students of restoration, art history and chemistry, and even a few retired professors who had known Bellini for forty years. In the back row, Matei was holding Viola, under strict orders to leave at the first "guadda" that was too loud.

In the front row, on the other hand, were three people Giulia hadn't expected. Bellini, of course, in a jacket and tie, with his black notebook on his knees. Next to him, Davide, his hair combed for the occasion. And on the other side, Pietro, who had skipped football practice and convinced his teacher that a university lecture was worth three history lessons.

Backstage, five minutes before starting, Giulia's hands were frozen. Chiara, who had come along to help her with the slides, slipped something into her pocket without saying a word. Giulia felt it with her fingers: it was Ernesto's small brush, the one from the shelf. "Matei gave it to me this morning," Chiara whispered. "He said that if you needed courage, you only had to hold it tight." Giulia held it tight. Then she went up onto the stage.

Giulia began exactly as she had rehearsed. "First of all I'd like to thank the university for the invitation. Firstly I'll talk to you about the painting; secondly, about the discovery; finally, about the fundraiser." Her voice trembled a little. However, after the first slide, a photograph of the Burial before restoration, covered in a brown haze, her fear vanished. In front of that image she was no longer a speaker. She was a restorer, talking about her work.

She explained Caravaggio's technique, that is, his way of incising the ground before painting. She showed the solvents, the lamps, the microscopes. She also showed, one after another, the photographs of the cleaning: the red of the cloak reappearing, the light on the gravediggers' shoulders, the saint's face. The students took notes in silence. In fact, as Matei had said, that was mainly what they had come for.

Then came the X-ray. The small face of the hidden child appeared on the screen, with his curly hair and wide-open eyes. A different kind of silence fell over the hall. Giulia described the discussion with the Heritage Authority: on the one hand the temptation to show the discovery of the century, on the other respect for the painter's choice. And then she told them about Turi, the old sacristan, and his words: "If Caravaggio had wanted it to be seen, he wouldn't have covered it."

For the last part, the fundraiser, Giulia hadn't prepared any slides. She had just one photograph: the fish-shaped terracotta money box on the altar, with the sign Turi had written. She told them about Concetta's lemons, the fishermen, Assunta's neighbours, the railwaymen of Sibiu, the Florentine boy who had sold cakes. For example, she read Pietro's letter to Totò: "Even though we've never met, I'm the one who gave you your name. So you're a bit like my brother."

In the front row, Pietro went as red as a tomato and hid behind his rucksack. Three hundred people turned round to look at him. Someone started clapping, and a moment later the whole hall was applauding. Pietro, behind his rucksack, was smiling so hard his cheeks hurt.

At that moment an old professor in the third row stood up, leaning on his stick. He was over ninety. "Forgive the interruption," he said in a thin voice. "In 1966 I was a student. I shovelled mud in Santa Croce for two weeks. I remember an old restorer with a moustache and a boy from Bologna with a red bicycle. I never knew their names." Bellini turned round sharply. Giulia smiled. "Their names were Ernesto and Aldo," she said. "And Ernesto's grandson is sitting right in front of you."

"In conclusion," said Giulia, when the applause had died down, "a restoration isn't just technical work. It's also a story about people. Without the sacristan, the painting would have been ruined. Without the fishermen and the children, it wouldn't have been finished. And without an old professor who taught me to look, I wouldn't be here." She looked at Bellini. Bellini lowered his eyes to his black notebook, but Giulia saw the pen trembling between his fingers.

At the end came question time. One student asked what the hardest moment of the restoration had been. Another asked whether it was true that you had to look at a painting for five minutes before touching it. Then a young man at the back raised his hand and asked: "What do you think it takes to become a good restorer?"

Giulia hesitated. She had prepared a long answer, with three points: firstly, moreover, finally. But before she could speak, a small hand went up in the front row. It was Davide. He had never spoken in public in his life. He said, in his low voice, so that hardly anyone could hear: "You have to look. And not touch anything. At least at first." Then he sat down, red to the tips of his ears.

The microphone, however, had heard perfectly, and the sentence echoed through the whole hall. For a second nobody said anything. Then Bellini closed his black notebook, stood up, alone, and began to applaud. After him the other professors stood up, then the students, then everyone. In the back row, Viola, woken by the noise, looked at all those people on their feet and said, very loudly: "Guadda!" This time, nobody made her leave.

After the talk, instead of crowding round Giulia, half the students crowded round Davide. They wanted to see his notebook, ask him where he studied, find out if he did portraits to order. Davide, terrified, answered in monosyllables. Bellini, meanwhile, went up onto the stage and stopped next to Giulia. He shook her hand, formally, as colleagues do. "Well done, Esposito," he said. It was the first time in five years he had said so. Then, softly, he added: "And thank you for the old professor."

That evening, for their second anniversary, Matei and Giulia had dinner alone on the terrace, while Graziella looked after Viola. Matei gave her a small parcel. Inside was a pencil portrait: Giulia on the stage of the lecture hall, microphone in hand and the screen behind her. Davide had done it during the talk, without anyone noticing. Underneath, in his tiny handwriting, he had written a title: "In conclusion".

Giulia looked at it for a long time. Then she said: "Two years ago, in Sorrento, I was a Neapolitan restorer in a wedding dress that was too long. Today I spoke in front of three hundred people." "And tomorrow?" asked Matei. Giulia smiled. "Tomorrow, first of all, coffee at ten. Then, Chiara's Annunciation. And finally…" She looked at the stars above the Arno. "Finally, everything else. Which, as someone says, is a story about people."
